title: Datasets, Features and Labels
summary: Load a small fictional housing dataset, inspect it with .columns and .head(), mark every column as a feature or the label, and justify which column is the label.

segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

A machine-learning model learns how some columns of a table relate to one special column. The columns we know are the **features**; the column we want to predict is the **label**; every row is one **example** the model learns from. In this lab you load `houses.csv`, a fictional table of 30 houses with their size in square feet, number of bedrooms, location and price, and inspect it with `.columns` and `.head()`. You then mark each column as a feature or the label in a dictionary, split the table into the feature table `X` and the label column `y`, and write one or two sentences explaining why `price` is the label. The next lectures use exactly this X and y to train and test real models.

segments.title: Lab: features and the label in a housing dataset

lab.title: Features and the label in a housing dataset
lab.objective: Load houses.csv, inspect it, mark every column as a feature or the label, split it into X and y, and justify the label choice.
lab.instructions:
The file houses.csv (columns size_sqft, bedrooms, location, price; 30 rows) is in your working directory. Write a program that:

1. Loads it with pd.read_csv() into df.
2. Inspects it: prints Columns: followed by df.columns.tolist(), then print(df.head()), then Rows (examples): followed by len(df). Every row is one example the model will learn from.
3. Makes labels, a dictionary with one entry per column: the value is "feature" for a column we know in advance and "label" for the one we want to predict. Also make features, the list of the feature column names in file order, and label_column, the name of the label column.
4. Splits the table: X = df[features] (the feature table) and y = df[label_column] (the label column). Prints Features: followed by the list, Label: followed by the label name, X shape: followed by X.shape and y shape: followed by y.shape.
5. Stores justification, one or two sentences (at least 15 words) that say why that column is the label; use the word predict. Prints it as Why: <text>.

The first and last lines of the expected output are:
Columns: ['size_sqft', 'bedrooms', 'location', 'price']
...
Why: <your sentences>
lab.constraints: Use pandas. Keep the names df, labels, features, label_column, X, y and justification. labels must have exactly one "label" entry. No input().
lab.starter_code:
import pandas as pd

# 4. X = df[features] and y = df[label_column]. Print Features:, Label:, X shape: and y shape:

hints: df.columns.tolist() gives the column names as a list and df.head() shows the first five rows. Ask yourself: which column would be unknown for a brand-new house? That one is the label.
labels = {"size_sqft": "feature", "bedrooms": "feature", "location": "feature", "price": "label"}. features is the list of the three feature names and label_column = "price".

X = df[features] selects several columns (a DataFrame, shape (30, 3)); y = df[label_column] selects one column (a Series, shape (30,)). Then write justification = "price is the label because it is the value we want the model to predict ...".

lab.solution:
import pandas as pd

# 1. Load the dataset
df = pd.read_csv("houses.csv")

# 2. Inspect it
print("Columns:", df.columns.tolist())
print(df.head())
print("Rows (examples):", len(df))

# 3. The role of every column
labels = {"size_sqft": "feature", "bedrooms": "feature", "location": "feature", "price": "label"}
features = ["size_sqft", "bedrooms", "location"]
label_column = "price"

# 4. Split the table into features (X) and the label (y)
X = df[features]
y = df[label_column]
print("Features:", features)
print("Label:", label_column)
print("X shape:", X.shape)
print("y shape:", y.shape)

# 5. Why price is the label
justification = (
    "price is the label because it is the value we want the model to predict for a new house; "
    "size_sqft, bedrooms and location are features because we already know them before the sale."
)
print("Why:", justification)
